You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
The test "testStop3()" reveals that when parsing the command line arguments with `stopAtNonOption` set to true, tokens after a non-option long argument are expected to be treated as distinct arguments without splitting or token bursting.

Examining the `PosixParser.flatten()` method, which is responsible for processing the input arguments array, we see it iterates over each token. Tokens starting with `--` are inspected for an '=' character. If found, the token is split around '=' into two tokens and added separately (lines 114-117). Single hyphen tokens with length 2 are processed by `processOptionToken()`. Other tokens that need bursting are passed to `burstToken()`.

In the test case, one of the tokens is `--zop==1`. According to `flatten()`, this token gets split into `"--zop"` and `"=1"` and both are added as separate tokens. This happens even though `"--zop"` is presumably an unrecognized option (not defined in options). The parser then continues with further tokens and processes them, bursting tokens like `-abtoast`.

Inside `burstToken()`, if a character representing an option is recognized, it is added as a separate token with a prefixed hyphen. If the current option accepts an argument, the rest of the token is added as one token. However, if the character is not recognized as an option and `stopAtNonOption` is true, it calls `process()` with the rest of the token to treat it as a value instead of bursting.

The `process()` method, when called with a token and if there is no current option, sets `eatTheRest` to true and adds `"--"` plus the token as tokens. The `gobble()` method then uses the `eatTheRest` flag to keep adding remaining tokens as extras.

The problem is that the split of a long option containing '=' (e.g. `--zop==1`) happens early in `flatten()`. The token `"--zop"` is put into tokens, but since it's not recognized, the rest after '=' is split into its own token `"=1"`. The parser continues processing and bursting tokens after that instead of stopping or treating all remaining tokens as arguments. This results in unexpected bursting and splitting where the test expects them to be preserved as is.

The root cause is that once an unrecognized long option (with '=') is encountered and split, there is no mechanism to stop further token bursts or to preserve the following tokens as extra arguments. The `stopAtNonOption` flag is not respected fully in this scenario, leading to the parser incorrectly bursting or splitting tokens after an unrecognized long option.

In summary, the bug occurs because the token splitting in `flatten()` for long options containing '=' happens unconditionally without stopping or properly treating everything after a non-option long option as separate tokens. The bursting logic only applies to short options, and the stop-at-non-option logic is applied too late, after inappropriate splitting has already occurred.

Recent similar bug reports about "PosixParser keeps bursting tokens even if a non option character is found" support this conclusion that the parser does not correctly stop bursting or token splitting when it should.

This misbehavior causes testStop3() to fail, as the test expects 3 separate extra arguments after `--zop==1` token, but the parser splits or bursts tokens incorrectly, leading to fewer or merged tokens than expected.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
